articles.title: Goodbye to the Grifters Harry and Meghan
articles.author: Ryan Zickgraf
articles.content: Six years after “Megxit,” Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are reversing course — at least partially. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will reportedly return to Britain later this month for an extended stay, settling with their children Archie and Lilibet in a private residence outside London while the children attend British schools. They will retain their mansion in Montecito as well as a holiday home in Portugal, and remain nonworking royals, which sounds like a contradiction, but alas. No official explanation has been offered for this spectacular U-turn, but perhaps the prodigal son eventually tires of eating among the swine, or, in Harry’s case, of producing polo documentaries that no one watches. Regardless, let me say on behalf of the rest of America: Goodbye and good riddance. We thankfully still have little use for royals, as the No Kings rallies have proved about our gold-plated pretend emperor holding court in the White House. Plus, there’s very little to miss. Harry’s retreat to the UK is not exactly Odysseus returning to Ithaca, older and wiser, ready to reclaim his place on the throne. He didn’t battle witches or outwit gods or even, really, suffer in California in any way ordinary people would recognize as suffering. The fallen prince has only a diminished Netflix deal and several hours of unlistenable audio, and the only army that conclusively routed him was Spotify’s podcast division. And Montecito is far from war-torn Troy; it’s California’s wine-dipped coastal retreat for the rich and famous, which The New York Times has described as “pale, pricey, gently geriatric” (translation: white, rich, and old). There, in 2020, Harry and Meghan purchased a sprawling $14 million mansion (now valued at $29 million) that made their historic Frogmore Cottage in England look like a royal-themed Airbnb. To be fair, Harry and Meghan aren’t Henry VIII–level villains, and their original alibi for Megxit in 2020 was understandable on some basic human level: Buckingham Palace was cold and inflexible; the British tabloid press’s Eye of Sauron relentlessly kept tabs on Harry’s family’s every move; and who doesn’t want to marry for love? The problem is that Harry and Meghan did more than leave an unhappy situation to escape the confines of a decrepit institution. They built a grand theory of themselves, a vision in which the Crown was an unbearable weight, and royal life was the only force preventing their authentic, brilliant selves from flowering. Freed from these things, they would prove that they could be American meritocrats and reveal what they actually had to say. But in the end, what they had to say, it turned out, was mostly that being Harry and Meghan was very hard. Noblesse Oblige for the Streaming Age Their career plan followed a familiar route pioneered by the Clintons, the Obamas, and other political celebrities who decided that wielding power was merely a prelude to producing content about the responsible use of power. Every former president, first lady, prince, and duchess now seems to believe he or she has an inner Oprah Winfrey. They no longer wish to be merely influential; they must become influencers, teaching the rest of us about leadership, resilience, and, of course, empathy. It’s noblesse oblige for the streaming TV age. The Sussexes entered this racket at its most decadent moment. Netflix reportedly offered them a deal worth as much as $100 million. Spotify reportedly signed them for $20 million. Archewell Productions promised documentaries, scripted television, children’s programming, and inspirational audio. Harry and Meghan would become the new king and queen of liberal infotainment. What Six Years Produced Look at what six years of “finding their voice” actually produced. With Love, Meghan , the lifestyle show meant to relaunch the Duchess as an American Martha Stewart for the girlboss set, didn’t crack the platform’s top three hundred shows in its debut year, and its hyper-staged jam-making and floral arranging were mocked across every timeline it aired near. They were producers of the documentary Cookie Queens , about the empowerment of young girls becoming Thin Mint entrepreneurs, which opened in theaters earlier this month to $328,000 across 446 screens. They produced only one genuine hit: Harry & Meghan , Netflix’s 2022 documentary about their relationship with the royal family. It set a record for a Netflix documentary debut. It was also six hours of palace gossip, family recriminations, and therapeutic jargon — an Instagram story stretched to Homeric length. Nothing else approached its success, except for Harry’s memoir Spare , for the obvious reason that nothing else contained the royal family. The animated children’s series Pearl was canceled. Harry’s Polo failed to enter Netflix’s global top ten. The second season of With Love, Meghan failed to crack the platform’s top thousand in the second half. And the streaming giant pulled its backing from Meghan’s As Ever lifestyle brand — though you can still buy her $32 small jars of honey . Likewise, Meghan’s Archetypes podcast produced twelve episodes before Spotify ended its agreement with Archewell, prompting executive Bill Simmons to call the couple “f–king grifters.” Her subsequent podcast, Confessions of a Female Founder , lasted nine episodes and will not return for a second season. Meanwhile, Harry produced nothing original after a year of brainstorming with Spotify — unless you count his reported idea for a nationwide hot chocolate–tasting podcast. A lot of the content aimed to be earnestly woke, but for people who have stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Meghan’s Archetypes podcast dressed itself up as feminist reckoning while mostly just cataloging the indignities of being extremely rich and extremely famous, a kind of trickle-down celebrity feminism where the revolutionary act is a duchess admitting she, too, has felt underestimated. Harry, for his part, built Spare and a docuseries out of grievance, however clumsily: furious about racist tabloid coverage in one breath, while coolly recounting that he had killed twenty-five Taliban fighters — men he described as chess pieces removed from the board — in the next. Too many of their subsequent projects have been a flailing attempt to manufacture a second act out of nothing but self-regard, and audiences, unlike royal correspondents, are under no obligation to keep pretending it’s compelling. The Dragon Was the Story Harry has portrayed his battles with the British press as a quest to slay dragons. Meghan once compared him to Super Mario of all figures, the man who “slayed the dragon” and “saved the princess.” But the Sussexes’ Californian adventure suggests that the dragon was also the most interesting thing about them. Once Harry had rescued his princess from the palace, neither seemed to know what the rest of the story was supposed to be. Do not feel sorry for them. America offered them what it offers every aristocrat, politician, and reality star: the opportunity to reinvent themselves as content. It gave them streaming contracts, celebrity friends, acres of California sunshine, and more money than most producers could dream of. What it could not give them was a personality independent of the Crown. So welcome home, Harry and Meghan. Britain can have them. But spare us the heroic framing: Odysseus spent ten years trying to reach home; Harry just spent six trying to monetize why he left his.

articles.title: Troy Jackson. The right person, at the right moment.
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content: “He’d tell me he was gonna stay awake holding my hand all night, so that when morning came, I’d still be there for him … As if all the strength that [my son] had in that little hand could counter generations of corporate greed … ” That is from a speech Troy Jackson gave in 2014 that I will never forget. It was at the Democratic Convention in Bangor. He was running for Congress, lagging far behind the eventual primary winner, Emily Cain. It seemed clear he was going to lose, but I was curious what he would say. I had been friends with Troy for a decade at this point. We had served together on the Labor Committee in the Maine Legislature and while he was always a solid vote for the working class, and definitely knew BS when he heard it from the business community, he didn’t seem politically ambitious. He was a very nice guy, showing up every day and just doing his job for his constituents. We often teased each other about our backgrounds: Me, a rabble-rousing city-slicker representing the People’s Republic of Portland, him a hayseed from the socially conservative willy-wags next to the Canadian border. He taught me what a feller-buncher was and why a “town” in his district was named T8 R11, and I promised I’d protect him, if he was ever willing to venture to a place that actually had streetlights. Running for higher office just wasn’t on my bingo card for Troy – he didn’t seem like a populist firebrand who could channel the emotional weight of the working class. But then I heard that speech. Troy introduced himself by speaking about how every Sunday night he would prepare to leave for the woods for the week. Living paycheck to paycheck meant traveling far from his hometown of Allagash because paper companies kept bringing temporary Canadian workers across the border illegally to do the work his neighbors had been doing for generations near his home (corporations were able to undercut Maine workers with Canadian because Canada provides national health care). After packing his lunches, he would go in to see his four-year-old son to kiss him goodnight and say goodbye. His son, desperate to have his father stay, would hold Troy’s hand and ask him not to go. “He’d tell me he was gonna stay awake holding my hand all night, so that when morning came, I’d still be there for him. I used to watch him fight to stay awake, with his little hand wrapped around my thumb. As if by strength of his will alone, he could keep me at home. As if all the strength that he had in that little hand could counter generations of corporate greed that was keeping other young children in the St. John Valley from their parents. It was during those long Sunday nights, that would turn into early Monday mornings, that I stopped accepting things for the way that they were, and started thinking about the way that they should be.” You could hear a pin drop in the massive convention hall as Troy told this story. After it, the place erupted. The bulk of the rest of the speech was the standard populist fare Troy has been preaching ever since. Economic inequality. The shortcomings of capitalism. A fighter for those beaten down. A shield against the powerful and a voice for the voiceless. Heartfelt. Empathetic. However, that opening imagery is what I will never forget. It was not simply beautiful writing, it showed an intrinsic connection to what the working class feels under a capitalist system that could not care less about our families. That kind of empathy is all too rare in politicians. But seeing it in him that night a dozen years ago, tells me that Troy is exactly the person we need in the United States Senate. *** This story was originally published by The Beacon , a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. articles.title: How Maine Funds War
articles.author: Pine and Roses -- Maine DSA
articles.content: On February 28th, 2026, rockets could be heard over Tehran. On that day the US military in cooperation with their Israeli allies launched a first strike missile attack against the Islamic Republic of Iran. People watched in horror as loved ones were buried under the rubble or shredded by bombs. Those hoping to escape the destruction hid in their homes, though no place was safe. Military bases and schools alike were hit. When the dust settled many searched the wreckage. Some found the lifeless bodies of those they cared for, others did not. This scene is not an uncommon occurrence. In January the US invaded Venezuela, kidnapping the nation’s president and murdering 80 people . It has since strengthened the embargo on Cuba, cutting the Island nation off from oil, which is critical for the functioning of essential services like hospitals, leading to many unnecessary deaths. US actions across the globe have led to the suffering of millions of people. Maine is a part of the United States though few people consider our state’s involvement in foreign policy. However, Maine is deeply connected to the lives of people abroad. Not in some abstract way, but materially and directly through what our state funds and supports. This article hopes to show how Maine is not simply a passive supporter by merely being a part of the US but is in fact an active participant in the horrors wrought abroad and how there is a direct connection between Maine and these conflicts. It does not have to be this way. While massive political upheaval would need to occur in the US as a whole, there are steps we can take within our state to mitigate its involvement in the US war machine. To start off, we should understand Maine’s involvement with the US military. As of fiscal year 2024, the US military spends about 4.6 billion dollars in Maine. This is around 4.7 percent of the state’s GDP. Out of the major nations being threatened by the US right now, Maine’s military expenses are around 60% of the total military expenses of Iran. The amount spent on the US military in Maine alone is over 9 times that of Venezuela and over 35 times that of Cuba. Maine dwarfs these nations regarding military spending. Maine itself only makes up around 0.8 percent of total US military spending. To reiterate, less than 1% of the US military is enough to outspend Cuba’s military 35 times over. Yet they are still somehow considered a national security threat where we must starve its people to death in order to protect America. With all this money being pumped into Maine, where is it actually going? General Dynamics is one of the major military contractors in the state. It is the fourth largest military contractor in the US. In 2024 the US government gave it 191 million for an army contract in Saco. The company owns Bath Iron Works (BIW), which is another major player in the Maine economy. In 2025 BIW was the fourth largest private employer in the state ranging from 6,000 to 6,500 employees. It has been producing ships for the US military since 1884 and was bought by General Dynamics in 1995. It produces around half of all Arleigh Burke-Class Destroyers. As of 2019 BIW supports 69 ships which is around 75% of the nation’s surface combatants. Texas Instruments, the other major corporation producing for the military, has been operating in Maine since 2011 when it purchased National Semiconductor. Texas Instruments does not work directly for the government, instead it produces much of the machinery that is placed inside weapons of war without making those weapons itself. Places like BIW have to purchase the components they need from somewhere, and Texas Instruments serves as one of those companies. It’s established that there are multiple corporations within the state that produce tools of warfare. However, how are those tools actually used in the US’s wars of aggression? The USS Thomas Hudner (DDG-116) and the USS Stockdale (DDG-106) are both Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers, which finished being produced in 2009 and 2018, respectively. Both being produced at BIW and costing a combined total of around 2.5 billion. On January 3rd 2026, the US invaded Venezuela with the goal of violating the nation’s sovereignty to kidnap its leader in a ploy to push Venezuela back under US control. Both the USS Thomas Hudner and the USS Stockdale were active in the Caribbean during the attack. They had sent the USS Stockdale to the Caribbean all the way back in September when the US was blowing up Venezuelan fishing boats. Rosa González lived in the port city of Catia La Mar. During the night of the attack, she was sitting with her family watching the game show “La Ruleta de la Suerte.” After the show had ended Rosa headed up to bed. However, that night a US missile would hit the apartment, destroying parts of the building and setting other parts on fire. In the destruction, Rosa was crushed under a washing machine. Her family was able to bring her to a medical clinic, but by that point it was too late. The USS Spruance was built by BIW and finished in 2009, costing around 1 billion dollars to produce. On February 28th it took part in Operation Epic Fury where it launched Tomahawk missiles into Iran. This attack led to the bombing of an Iranian girls’ school and the murder of over 150 students. A Guardian article recounting eyewitness testimony of the attack describes a father going to a morgue to look for his daughter, “The headscarf that she was always so careful to pin in place – just so – had slipped. ‘Her head was broken,’ he says. Her ribs, too, had caved in. But the rest of her body was still intact. She was covered with dust. That’s her, he told the morgue staff: her name is Zahra Behroozi. She was eight years old.” The weapons produced in Maine are directly involved in the atrocities the US commits abroad. There is no separation between domestic and foreign policy. Our domestic military industries are built on the murder of others. It is because of the funding and support that we give to these industries that innocent civilians abroad, including thousands of children, are killed. We cannot separate these facts. There is no position of “good on domestic policy but bad on foreign policy.” While the government and businesses spend billions to kill innocents abroad, ten of millions at home cannot get access to proper healthcare, are unable to buy a house or afford rent, and are struggling to pay for basic necessities. I stated at the beginning of this article that as of fiscal year 2024, the government spends around 4.6 billion dollars on the war industry in Maine. This amount could easily fund the national parks in Maine and could fully fund all the national parks in the US with over a billion to spare. It could also fully fund SNAP within the state which costs only around 348 million dollars yearly. On top of this, it could also pay for General Assistance (GA) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) which cost around 36 million and 142 million , respectively. We could fund all of these programs at the same time and we would still have around half a billion left over. One of the main arguments against shutting down these war industries is that they are major employers. BIW is the fourth largest employer in the state of Maine with over 6,000 people. Which does not count all the people employed in industries which build the materials and technology that is bought by BIW and companies like it. However, this does not mean that these industries need to continue in their current form. Places like BIW could transition to civilian ship production. The government could utilize all the money it was spending on war assistance in this transition as well as help fund and develop other industries in the state to create jobs for people. Just because these major employers participate in the military war complex it does not mean they have to be or always will be. There are many things like the development of public transportation and renewable energy which could be massive employers within the state. The US has the money to create this transition as long as we do not spend it on war and death. As an example, a proposed rail line between Portland and Westbrook would cost an estimated 100 million , taking up only 2% of the military spending in Maine while establishing much needed public transportation in the area. A plan proposed by Acadia Center back in 2018 to invest in Maine’s transportation said it could bring in over 8,700 new jobs, as well as 3.8 billion in economic benefits. On top of new jobs, robust public transportation would give tens of thousands of people more options to engage with the wider Maine community. Over 90 thousand people over the age of 18 in Maine do not own a driver’s license. Investing in public transportation would mean that people would not be at risk of missing a doctor’s appointment because they do not have access to a vehicle. We could also build offshore wind turbines, which would both help build renewable power and also supply jobs. It would cost around 760 million , or around 17% of military spending in the state. The Turbines are projected to create 6,000 jobs during construction and 1,000 jobs annually. They would also bring in 1.1 billion in economic activity just through construction. These examples show moderate changes that could be made which, while not eliminating the crisis suffered by working Mainers, would definitely help alleviate it. So if what the US spends on the war industry in Maine were redirected to actually help people and benefit society, why isn’t it? Because it is not in the interests of the people in power to do so. The US is built on imperialism, companies and government officials can get rich off of endless wars which fuel the defense industry and its profits. On top of this, businesses can make massive amounts of wealth by exploiting the labor and resources of other nations. Why employ people in the US when you can underpay workers abroad? There is no interest in genuinely helping people in the US, only winning them over through cheap products often made with foreign slave labor so they will continue to support the US’s imperialist project abroad. If there is a genuine desire to gain things like universal healthcare or stable living conditions for workers in the US, then anti-imperialism must be at the heart of the movement. If it is not, concessions will only serve to further the murder of the global south and any gains made will be lost when the next inevitable economic crisis emerges. The US government has more than enough money to feed people. However, people will continue to go hungry as long as there are incentives to pour that money into war. If we want to truly make Mainers’ lives more affordable then we have to dismantle the US war machine. The post How Maine Funds War appeared first on Pine & Roses .

articles.title: The Road to Power: A Socialist Guide to Winning in America
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: The following is an excerpt from the upcoming book “The American Road to Socialism: The Unfinished Struggle for Democracy” Ask an American whether workers should own the results of their labor, and you will get a yes. Ask whether the economy is rigged in favor of corporations and the wealthy, and you will get a yes – 70 percent of respondents in a national poll last year, including 58 percent of Republicans, said the system is rigged and needs to be replaced. Ask whether your boss, your landlord, and your insurance company have too much control over your life, and you will get a yes. Then say the word “socialism,” and watch the yes turn into a maybe. That gap is the central strategic problem we in the American left face. This is a challenge we socialists have faced for decades, but the political foundations are changing. Sixty-two percent of Americans under thirty now hold a favorable view of socialism. Among Democrats , favorable views have climbed from 50 percent in 2010 to 66 percent in 2025. Meanwhile Gallup found the approval rate of capitalism slipping to 54 percent, its worst showing in over a decade of polling. Roughly 15 percent of 2024 Trump voters — younger, more racially diverse, and largely disengaged from politics — told pollsters they prefer democratic socialism to capitalism. These results have been matched with equal intensity in the waves of socialist primary victories across the country this cycle. DSA endorsed roughly 150 candidates in 2026. By the end of June, thirty-five had won their primaries or gone unopposed . These wins are only the beginning of building a durable socialist movement in this country. If we are to displace the political establishment rather than merely embarrass it, we have to build a movement that crosses the partisan spectrum. Closing the gap between what Americans already believe and what they think socialism is takes three things: understanding why the gap exists, learning to speak in a way that closes it, and building an organization disciplined enough to contest the communities where the gap will be closed. Why Has America Not (Yet) Embraced Socialism? We first have to address the elephant in the room: Why over the 250 years of this country’s existence has socialism failed to take root? There are four structural obstacles in this country that have historically prevented the United States of America from embracing socialism. First, the deliberate repression of the left by capital and the state cannot be ignored when answering this question. McCarthyism, COINTELPRO, the destruction of radical unions, elite-driven cultural backlash to eras of progressive political dominance, and the outright assassination of prominent leftist leaders in this country have all been tools used by the elite to prevent the destruction of capitalism. Second is elite-driven racial divisiveness. In a multiracial society like ours, racism has been the most reliable instrument the political and economic elite have for keeping the working class divided against itself, deployed by reactionary coalitions from the founding of this country, through the end of Reconstruction, the Dixiecrats and the Southern Strategy, and present day racial divides. When workers are pitted against each other, they cannot organize alongside one other against the capitalist minority. Third, unlike almost every other industrialized democracy, the United States has for most of its history lacked a durable labor or socialist party, leaving the working class without an independent political vehicle to organize. The Socialist Party, as well as the Democratic Party at certain points in its history, offered a space for working class political organization. But this wasn’t permanent. The structural explanation for this absence lies in the American electoral system itself. Winner-take-all elections, single-member congressional districts, and the Electoral College create nearly insurmountable barriers to third parties that simply do not exist in the proportional representation systems of Europe and Latin America. The fourth obstacle is closely related to the third—the cultural identification of socialism with foreign ideologies and anti-Americanism. For a century, the right has successfully branded socialism as something alien to the American tradition: a European import at best and Soviet totalitarianism at worst. This branding has been reinforced by a corporate-controlled media apparatus that has consistently marginalized socialist voices from mainstream political discourse while amplifying the association between socialism and authoritarianism. This is the obstacle that matters most, because all others can be overcome through organizing, institution-building, and political strategy. If Americans continue to believe socialism is fundamentally un-American, no amount of doorknocking will overcome that barrier. The cultural and rhetorical reframing of socialism that we present to the masses is the foundation everything else rests on. Speaking American: How We Talk About Socialism The reason why socialism in this country has failed to take off isn’t because Americans reject its core premises, but because they reject its branding. When we describe the actual tenets of democratic socialism: workers controlling their workplaces, affordable housing, universal healthcare, strong communities, freedom from corporate domination, etc., polls consistently show majority support among Americans. What Americans reject is the word socialism and the cultural associations it carries. The task is therefore to show them that what they already want is socialism. We can achieve this goal through five cultural and rhetorical strategies. The most effective brand of political communication is narrative rather than argumentative. People are not persuaded by policy papers, ideological frameworks, or abstract appeals to justice. What persuades voters are stories that connect political ideas to lived human experiences. When a worker describes watching the company they spent twenty years building get sold out from under them so that a private equity firm could extract its assets, that story makes the case for cooperative ownership more powerfully than any theoretical argument ever could. When a single mother describes choosing between filling a prescription and paying rent, that story makes the case for universal healthcare in terms no policy brief can match. Socialists must learn to lead with stories because stories create the emotional connection that opens people to ideas they might otherwise reject on ideological grounds. This is the basis of agitation as a political strategy—the simple act of using leading questions and “whose side are you on” to bring voters to your desired outcome—which then opens voters to political organizing. The American Dream with Socialist Characteristics Socialism isn’t a rejection of the American Dream, but is instead its ultimate fulfillment. The dream as originally conceived—that through hard work, anyone can build a good life in this country—has been hollowed out by capitalism. When wages stagnate, housing is unaffordable, healthcare bankrupts families, and student debt crushes an entire generation, the promise of a better life becomes a cruel joke for the working American. Socialism restores the American Dream by giving Americans the material security to actually turn their hard work into a higher standard of living. This is how we should communicate our vision to the American public—not as a radical departure from what they’ve been promised, but as a radical fulfillment of the promise they have known their whole lives. It is through socialism that the life of a happy family, a happy home, a good job, and a Fourth of July barbecue can be realized for the working majority of this country. You Do the Work, You Own the Results Producerism is the belief that those who produce wealth should get to control wealth. Producerism should be at the rhetorical and policy center of our movement. In a country where voters pride themselves on hard work, hard work should be rewarded. Socialism accomplishes this by giving workers control over their own labor. No longer is there surplus labor value for capitalists to extract. What you create is what you control. Producerism has deep roots in the American political tradition from Jefferson, Jackson, and the Populists all the way through the labor movement, the New Deal, and the Great Society. The twenty-first century version of this argument is simple: you produce the wealth, you should own it. Corporate executives, Wall Street traders, and trust fund inheritors produce nothing. Instead, they extract wealth from Americans who work for a living. Socialism—which is fundamentally the belief that workers should control the wealth they create—isn’t a foreign import. Cooperative ownership is the logical conclusion of the producerist principle that Americans have believed in for two centuries. When we talk to voters, we should frame our project as “we believe the people who do the work should own the results of their work.” That is a sentence that virtually every American will agree with, and it is the most basic definition of socialism. Your Neighbor is Not Your Enemy Americans have a deep attachment to community, whether religious, familial, neighborhood, or civic. Barn raisings, mutual aid societies, the labor union, and the tradition of neighbors helping neighbors were all core institutions of American culture hollowed out by capitalism. Capitalism has left the American worker small, isolated, and unable to defend themselves against either an abusive employer or an indifferent state. Cooperatives, tenant unions, and popular assemblies are the tools ordinary people use to rebuild that. Socialism is what happens when neighbors decide to look out for each other instead of leaving everyone to fend for themselves. Us Against the Oligarchs The defining feature of American politics right now is that voters across the spectrum are furious at elites. The right channels that fury at cultural figures, immigrants, and minorities. Our job is to channel it to the economic elites who actually control people’s lives. Democratic socialism is not “big government.” It is the opposite of oligarchy: a system where ordinary people hold power instead of billionaires. Every proposal we make should be framed as transferring power from elites to working people, not from the private sector to the state. Americans distrust both big business and big government, and our answer is therefore neither. Socialism is the democratic self-governance of working people, which is what the natural conclusion of the values most Americans ascribe to the founding of this country. What Freedom Really Means This is the framing we underuse most. The right insists socialism means the government running your life. In reality it is the capitalist class running it. Your boss controls your time, your wages, your conditions. Your landlord controls your housing. Your insurance company controls whether you get treatment. There is no meaningful freedom when every condition of your survival depends on the decisions of unaccountable private actors. Democratic socialism offers two freedoms at once: the freedom that comes from a baseline of material security, and the freedom that comes from actual control over your workplace, your building, and your neighborhood. What could be more American than that? “The Party Within the Party” That brings us to the question every American socialist has to answer: what do we do with the Democratic Party? Make a clean break and start a third party, or organize inside? The answer is both: the “party within the party.” This strategy is not new or revolutionary for the DSA, but it could use some sharpening and clarity. Building a third party under current conditions is not possible given the design of our electoral system and the entrenchment of the duopoly. When those conditions change, likely through our own efforts, so should our approach. But working within the Democratic Party carries its own risks. Without an independent organizational base we will be absorbed and neutralized, which is exactly what happened to progressive movements throughout the twentieth century. I can’t say when the DSA will reach a state where it can truly break from the Democrats and its bourgeois politics, but our goal is not to become Democrats. Instead, we must use Democrats’ existing infrastructure to build our own power and base of support. What we therefore need is an independent socialist organization with its own membership, funding, discipline, and platform. We can and should use the Democratic ballot line as a vehicle to win elections, gain national publicity, and push for reforms to the political system. As we do so, we will win over the sympathy of left-leaning voters while retaining the independence to hold our own officials accountable, mobilize outside election cycles, and build working-class institutions that outlast any party. In order to accomplish this, we must do three things: streamline our endorsement process, run for and win smaller local and state offices, and expand our fight to contest elections in more rural and conservative parts of the country. The Endorsement Process Ours should be an endorsement that candidates actively seek out, not one selectively and arbitrarily given. Right now the process is often slow, contentious, and dominated by factional dynamics that prioritize ideological alignment over strategic opportunity. Candidates substantively aligned with democratic socialist principles get denied because they fail to check a few boxes in our process, and races go uncontested by socialists because nobody clears the purity threshold. A strategically oriented process would test candidates against a short list of non-negotiables — economic democracy, racial justice, anti-militarism, labor rights — allow flexibility on secondary questions, and prioritize races we can actually win. The Local Governance Gap There are thousands of offices in this country decided by a few hundred or even a few dozen votes: city councils, county boards, township trustees, school boards, water reclamation districts, planning commissions. They are not glamorous. They generate no national press. They are also where the governance that shapes working people’s daily lives actually happens. A single organized chapter can win them with minimal resources. Winning them turns municipal and state governments into laboratories of socialist policy — and, just as importantly, makes voters comfortable with the idea of socialists governing, because they can see it working down the street. It is also how we build a bench. You do not produce candidates capable of competing at the highest level without officeholders who have already governed something. DSA’s habit of pouring electoral energy into high-profile congressional races while neglecting the offices where socialism can be practiced most tangibly is a strategic failure that caps our growth. Purple & Red Territory Fifty-eight percent of Republicans think the economy is rigged for the rich. Of the respondents who had never heard of DSA, 43 percent were more amenable to democratic socialism against 38 percent for capitalism — meaning our brand problem is, in a real sense, an introduction problem. Bernie Sanders and AOC draw enormous crowds in places where we currently have limited resources and support. These are communities where a candidate running the producerist message alongside concrete local issues — housing costs, healthcare access, job quality — can win, particularly in local and state races where national partisan dynamics matter least. The proof of concept of the socialist electoral model is no longer hypothetical, and it is no longer only applicable in progressive areas like New York. Zohran Mamdani started at 1 percent in the polls and beat the entire New York establishment twice, winning 30 percent of the districts Trump carried in 2024 — not because those voters had a conversion experience, but because Mamdani was the only candidate talking about their rent. Donavan McKinney just won a congressional primary in Detroit with a fraction of his opponent’s money, running on working-class representation in government, taxing the wealthy, and getting corporate cash out of politics. Neither man asked anyone to become a socialist. Our candidates have won by speaking to material conditions and letting the label take care of itself. They are using their success in office to bring people into socialism by example. That is a replicable model, and we have been rationing it. Imagine every chapter with a few hundred members identifying one winnable local race, recruiting a candidate committed to the platform, and running a real field operation. Expanding the Project But how do we accomplish all of these goals? There are several ways in which we can go about expanding the reach of the DSA organization which mostly entail building upon already existing programs. The Socialists in Office program (SIO) is a DSA-sponsored program that coordinates with and supports DSA officials in public office through a co-governance model. The organization works with SIOs on building coalitions with key communities, teaching our politicians the ropes of local governance, and on drafting and passing legislation. The SIO program has been incredibly effective at building a base of socialist politicians with strong constituent services and strong legislative skills, but the program could be significantly expanded. Imagine if the SIO program was involved in the electoral process before candidates won their races? The program should be the primary vehicle by which we elect socialists across the country. It should work with candidates during their campaigns, providing media training, fundraising support, and organizing training. It should work to build coalitions between DSA candidates and key groups like labor, students’ groups, and tenants’ organizations. And it should be involved in identifying candidates across the country to run for office under the DSA banner. But engaging in electoralism alone will not be enough to move the masses towards socialism. In essence, the DSA must break from the two-party tradition of only showing up in communities when it comes time for Americans to vote. DSA cadres must be continually present in communities, doing the work of building strong relations with local residents. As we expand our organizing capacity, we should engage in mutual-aid work, providing communities with key services that corporations and governments refuse to offer. From the public housing complex to the barn-house, we must be in the communities that will decide the future of this country, becoming a key resource for local residents without ever asking for a vote or donation in return. This is how we, and by extension socialism, can become the most trusted political project in this country. The road to socialism here will not be paved by one election, one candidate, or one project. It will be built by the sustained, unglamorous work of people who refuse to accept that the richest country in human history cannot provide a dignified life for everyone in it. The framings and arguments above are a toolkit to be adapted to the conditions of communities across the country. The question is no longer whether socialism can win in America. It is whether we are willing to do the work to achieve that victory. The post The Road to Power: A Socialist Guide to Winning in America appeared first on Midwest Socialist .

articles.title: You Aren’t Special – and Neither am I
articles.author: Cleveland DSA
articles.content: by Alex K. Many of the arguments I have heard against the Participatory Democracy proposal boil down to one simple phrase: “What if I can’t participate?”. Often a theoretical member who works the night shift, or is taking care of family members, or cannot attend these meetings for a myriad of reasons is given as to why Participatory Democracy is not only unfair, but akin to a poll tax or a literacy test. I would ask why the Cleveland DSA is required to replicate Liberal voting structures in an organization that looks to create a system outside of the current oligarchy built upon centuries of white supremacy, misogyny, and outdated Enlightenment ideals. Voting should be the end process of a long period of conversation, deliberation, and, most importantly, organizing. I dare those reading this to try and think outside of the individualist society that so many of us have grown up in to think of voting not as a question of “What happens if I cannot vote?”, but as a question of “Am I organizing effectively enough to trust my comrades who can?”. While the title of this article, “You Aren’t Special – And Neither Am I” is meant to be inflammatory, I challenge the reader to think of Cleveland DSA not as an organization made up of individuals, but as an organized mass that is anchored in the idea that the collective is always stronger than the sum of its parts–of which voting is only one minor part. As a Marxist, and a part of the Marxist Unity Group (MUG), I am interested in theories of Democracy and the ways that we can make our structures more Democratic, and I reject the idea that the ultimate form of Democracy is casting a ballot. Patricia Springborg notes that Marx sees the “positive case for democracy as bearing a peculiar and intimate relation to politics and its emergence as a historically specific cultural complex–a uniquely intimate relationship that is not shared by other regimes such as monarchies and aristocracies.”(1) Though this may seem complex at first, the crux of Marx’s argument is simple: Democracy is more than existing under a political system, it is about being able to have a true, meaningful relationship to the way that a person interacts with and shapes their own political system. While this point may seem to express, at the very least, sympathy towards One Member One Vote, Springborg expands on this basis to show that there is more to Democracy than the simple act of voting. There are two additional points that Springborg makes about Marx’s views on democracy: one is that “democracy does not require the participation of all members of society as individuals in the decision-making process and that, therefore, the debate over the relative merits of direct or representative democracy is misdirected.”(2) This goes hand-in-hand with the final argument Springborg describes–“political participation turns not on the function of deputies or representatives but rather on political suffrage,” and in quoting Marx, reiterates that “Voting, ‘considered philosophically … is the immediate, the direct, the existing and not simply imagined relation of civil society to the political state.’”(3) Together, these arguments paint a picture of Democracy based on a foundation of universalism, rather than individualism. Democracy does not come about through giving everyone a day off to cast a ballot. Rather, it is essential that everyone can cast a ballot, but that casting a ballot comes about through people having a deep connection to what they are voting on, understanding that part of democracy is that not everyone who is able to participate does participate, and that voting is a political act–not the political act. Marx clearly states that if members of the state–or perhaps Cleveland DSA if you are so inclined–“are an integral part of the state, then it is obvious that their social existence is already their actual participation in it. They are not only integral parts of the state, but the state is their integral part.”(4) Those who choose to be in Cleveland DSA are an integral part of it, and it is notable that being part of Cleveland DSA is a unique choice that exists outside of, though not independent from, the larger American political sphere. Springborg expands on Marx’s rejection of the separation between the self and the state in how focusing on individual political actions as “all” or “not all” “falsely presumes the political to be constituted by single political acts performed by individuals, focusing exclusively on the legislature as the locus of popular participation.”(5) Voting is the ultimate realization of a single political act performed by an individual. I challenge all persons in Cleveland DSA to think beyond themselves to a politic based on all of us, together, regardless of a single person’s circumstances. In writing this, I look to challenge ideas of what it means to vote as a member of Cleveland DSA, outside of the historical understanding of what Democracy can, and should, look like. What does it mean to be Democratic as the systems made to suppress and silence political engagement are potentially replicated in Cleveland DSA? In an organization whose program clearly states that “[The Democratic Socialists of America] are workers fighting to transform society: to win the battle for democracy, draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic,”(6) it is essential to look beyond American individualism and the idea that the ultimate form of Democracy is exemplified through a ballot. I do not believe that replicating the same systems that have not only failed us, but were designed to oppress and suppress, will create the future we all look towards. It is only through meaningful, powerful organizing that the systems we look to transform can truly change: not through the vote of a single individual. Footnotes 1 Patricia Springborg, “Karl Marx on Democracy, Participation, Voting, and Equality,” Political Theory 12, no.4 (1984): 538: http://www.jstor.com/stable/191498 2 Springborg, “Karl Marx on Democracy,” 538. 3 Springborg, “Karl Marx on Democracy,” 538. 4 Karl Marx, “Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right,” §§ 308 Civil Society and the Estates, Marxist Internet Archive, accessed August 19, 2026, https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1843/critique-hpr/ch06.htm 5 Springborg, “Karl Marx on Democracy,” 542. 6 Democratic Socialists of America, “Our Program,” section “Our Perspective” paragraph 5, accessed August 19, 2026, https://program.dsausa.org/ The post You Aren’t Special – and Neither am I appeared first on Democratic Socialists of America .

articles.title: Put AI Under Social Ownership for Social Purposes
articles.author: Peter Dorman
articles.content: A lively debate has been taking place in Jacobin over what to do about artificial intelligence. AI is clearly a technology with potential for enormous benefit and harm — and perhaps both at the same time. Financially, it could put even more income in the hands of billionaires, or it could produce a bubble the implosion of which pushes the net worth of investors, innocent and guilty alike, off a cliff. Either way, it needs to be redirected away from narrow financial imperatives and toward social ends, and this requires a change in ownership. But what change, and how? The obvious go-to for socialists is to give government a controlling interest, and that’s what Bernie Sanders has proposed : use a onetime tax to transfer half the equity in US-based AI companies to a new sovereign wealth fund, which would then have veto power over future decisions affecting the technology while sharing in the profits it generates. But there is also unease with the idea, not least because Donald Trump has also floated federal ownership stakes — and even a remote similarity is grounds for suspicion. More precisely, given the state of American democracy and the grotesque imbalance of political power favoring the ultrarich, it is reasonable to doubt that a large public stake would yield the outcomes we want to see from it. To design social ownership so it truly reflects social purposes in a globalizing world, we need to rethink the issue from the ground up. Just why do we need to remove ownership and control from the hands of wealthy investors? Exactly what changes are we trying to bring about? The Why and How of Public Ownership The first question has a three-part answer. First, we are suffering from the overbearing power of an oligarchy that transforms vastly excessive wealth into suffocating political and social influence. If AI generates the economic benefits advertised for it, even greater riches will follow. AI companies convert vast stores of collectively produced knowledge and culture, along with publicly supported research, into private wealth. If AI does produce the economic benefits its exponents promise, those gains should be broadly shared rather than accrue to a small group of plutocrats. Second, the breakneck pursuit of market domination is generating immense costs while failing to deliver benefits that can’t be readily marketized. It is undertaken either nakedly for enrichment or in the name of a perverse, zero-sum notion of patriotism (any loss of market share to Chinese companies, some say, imperils America’s “national security”). Finally, AI is a complex, rapidly evolving technology, and, as such, it is almost impossible to regulate. Yes, broad regulations on the use of AI and the resources it vacuums up are feasible and should be enacted as soon as possible. Personally, I’d begin with a prohibition on any chatbot or similar program using the first person in its messaging: “I” is a lie. But regulation of how models are trained, how they respond to prompts, and how they may soon be integrated with reasoning engines — these matters are almost impossible to regulate from the outside. It’s a game of never-ending catch-up that regulators, even if aggressive and well-motived, are unlikely to win. So, to sum up the why , we need to share the wealth, dial back the profit motive, and incorporate public regulation within the enterprises developing and applying AI. Which brings us to the crucial problem of how . Public ownership would deal with the first problem, and no doubt that’s a major reason why Sanders and others want to take this step. It might also help with the third, since, if nothing else, the government as equity investor could demand that all information relevant to regulation be made public in real time. Those are both significant advantages that should not be disparaged. But public ownership also poses problems of its own. One, as a previous Jacobin writer correctly emphasized , is that government control and democratic control are typically quite far apart. Even in the best of circumstances, people get to vote only periodically for political representatives. By the time decision-making snakes its way down to lower levels in the bureaucracy the democratic mandate is weak. And today those circumstances are light years from democratic perfection. Public Pluralities Yet the problem with public ownership is even more fundamental. To see it, we need to think concretely about what it is we want AI to do — and not do — and ask how ownership models alone can resolve potential conflicts. Here are several issue areas that occur to me: Privacy and personal freedom . AI is being deployed to create systems of private and public surveillance without equal in human history. This ranges from surveillance pricing, where what we pay is a function of what an AI agent determines we are willing to pay, to state profiling of our political values for purposes of social control. A frightening prospect is the use of AI to target and annihilate places and people beyond human oversight, as exemplified by Israel’s Lavender program. Management and employment . Much of the putative economic value of AI stems from its claimed ability, now or soon, to assume direct management of businesses, government agencies, and other organizations, with the wholesale dismissal of the human beings who now do this work. That can lead to frustratingly unresponsive or unhelpful services — an aspect of Cory Doctorow’s enshittification — and of course it raises the specter of mass unemployment. Yet replacing drudgery with automation can also be an enormous social boon; just think of the millions of secretaries whose typing, filing, and other repetitive clerical chores were taken over by word processing apps. (I was in their ranks once.) Key choices about how organizations should be run, and who will be needed to run them, are at stake. Environment and resources . Unlike earlier iterations of digital technology, AI makes massive, almost mind-boggling demands on our water resources, energy systems, and rare minerals. This is due to its brute-force training methods, and it might be mitigated by more specialized training combined with greater use of logic. In any case, there are important issues to resolve about how to trade off computing capacity and resource use, along with whose resources should be tapped and how they should be compensated for them. Applications across society . As much as attention has focused on the issues above, this may be just as important in the long run. Already educators are struggling with the slash-and-burn effects of AI on classrooms. The impacts on writing, music, and visual culture could be enormously positive, negative, or (most likely) both. AI shows great promise in research, but a lot will depend on whether it augments our understanding of the fields to which we apply it, or simply pulls results out of a black box. This would matter even if agents were perfectly reliable, which they’re not. Who can we trust to design these applications in a way that expands our potential as learners and creators? There are important conclusions to draw from even this cursory survey. One is that many kinds of choices must be made. Some are distributive — who gains, who loses — but others involve fundamental values. Another is that, given the many dimensions of AI’s future development, it’s impossible to specify a single public interest that all of us would agree to sign onto. It’s difficult to overstate how important it is to understand this. The public whose interests should guide us is the actually existing one, with all its diversity of attitudes and priorities — not an imaginary public in which everyone thinks just the way you or I do. Even if everyone in the United States adopted progressive values, choices would still have to be made among competing priorities. The issue is not data centers everywhere versus nowhere, or AI-generated documents versus only human-written ones, or any other dichotomous choice. It is about priorities, emphases, adjustments, and reimagined designs. The current choices are mercenary and terrible, but there is no simple alternative upon which everyone will agree. Purposeful Ownership So we need not only democracy in the AI world but also true pluralism: different implementations existing side by side from which we can choose. This is also necessary for standard economic reasons, since we won’t know in advance what approaches to the development of AI will turn out to be best, either in technical or social terms. Again, pluralism. Fortunately, we already have the beginnings of the alternative we need: ownership by purpose trusts. Up to now, this has progressed one retirement at a time, as public-minded owners such as Patagonia’s Yvon Chouinard, who chose to place control of their companies in the hands of trustees legally bound to protect particular purposes. In the case of Patagonia, this was an environmental commitment . Under the stronger version of the model proposed here, profit would become a means, not an end. The trust deed would stipulate that earnings, after necessary reinvestments, be devoted to advancing the firm’s overriding purposes rather than distributed to private investors. If you scan a directory of such firms, you’ll find a variety of mandatory purposes, ranging from worker benefit to community development to enhancing local food systems, with many designating more than one of them. Which is how it should be: we are a diverse society, and our purposes are many and do not always lead to the same choices. However, to adapt this model to AI we need to make two very large changes. First, the public, acting through its elected representatives, would have to initiate the conversion of existing firms to purpose trusts. This would require a process for recruiting trustees and, above all, financing the purchase of firms’ equity. Some form of tax on profits would obviously be essential. Second, the purposes would need to be chosen not by enlightened, aging entrepreneurs but by society itself. Because multiple trusts could coexist, they could pursue a range of purposes that would not always agree with one another. Some roughly democratic method would be needed to ensure that the allocation of funding among the trusts corresponds to the proportion of the community that supports respective purposes. A side note: Anthropic is not itself a trust, but its governance structure includes a long-term benefit trust . It differs from the mode described here in several crucial ways: investors maintain their claims on profits; Anthropic’s mandate was focused on the long-term risks posed by AI, leaving most business questions unaddressed. It is relatively easy for equity owners to dissolve the trust whenever they wish. It is no secret that Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering. The Purpose-Trust Advantage Another big advantage of the purpose-trust approach over public ownership is that it is far better suited to handle the pushes and pulls of the global economy. It can partner with foreign firms if it chooses. It can pursue international strategies consistent with its purposes separate from the passing predilections of politicians — a huge consideration since China is also a key player. And it can use these relationships to promote people-serving purposes beyond our borders, which can add a potentially progressive twist to globalization. This flexibility follows from the model: once capitalized, trust-owned firms are operationally autonomous and governed by their legally binding purposes. This last point is key. Consider a trust-owned AI firm whose legally binding objective is to help users be more creative and productive. This would obligate the firm to develop tools that enhance user’s capacities and to prohibit the development of applications that are routinizing or disempowering. But such a broad purpose could only be realized through sustained interaction with users. Some of this would take the form of standard market feedback, as when a gardener buys an AI helper that makes gardening more worthwhile, or someone learning a new language purchases an AI teaching tool. Our hypothetical trust-owned business would still have to earn enough revenue to cover its costs, just like everyone else. Now imagine that its tools were intended for use by people at work, making it possible for unions and professional or advocacy groups to have a voice in their design and deployment. Organizations of all sorts could partner with our AI developer, since trust ownership is a form of social ownership that preserves the firm’s independence. One trust-owned firm could also collaborate with another when their missions overlap, or if they operate in related parts of the economy — for example, an AI developer joining forces with a pharmaceutical company, with both owned by purpose trusts. And, as mentioned above, national borders do not set boundaries on these kinds of partnerships unless specific laws are passed to regulate them. Conversely, two trust-owned firms with opposed missions might compete if they’re in the same market — not to amass the greatest possible profit but to advance their respective missions. This would be social ownership without the myth of a homogenous, same-thinking society. Of course, unlike public ownership, social ownership via purpose trusts does not come ready-made. We have limited experience to draw on, and important questions remain unanswered. There will surely be a learning curve. But the need for a vibrant, diverse, and purpose-driven alternative economy is more urgent than ever, and the way to figure it out is to start creating it.
