articles.title: Can Tenant Organizing Build Political Power? The DSA Experience
articles.author: Boston DSA
articles.content: [[{“value”:” By: Steve Dubb This article was originally published by Shelterforce on August 12, 2026. In the world of movement organizing, few groups in the past decade have undergone a faster demographic transition or greater growth than the Democratic Socialists of America, better known as DSA. Between 2015 and 2017, boosted by Sen. Bernie Sanders’s 2016 presidential campaign, the average age of DSA members dropped from 64 to about 30, and membership tripled from 8,000 to about 25,000, according to Washington Post reporting . Growth has continued since then. As of December 2025, DSA reportedly had 92,912 members —more than 10 times the number from a decade earlier. DSA is best known for its electoral organizing. Famously, last year, in New York City, the local DSA chapter played a major role in supporting the successful mayoral campaign of Zohran Mamdani. But DSA’s organizing extends far beyond elections. A significant number of local DSA chapters have adopted tenant organizing as a focus of their work. In some communities, the local tenant union and the DSA tenant organizing working group are one and the same. More often, DSA housing organizers and tenant unions are close allies, though they operate independently of each other. A motivating factor for DSA members is the opportunity to use organizing to make a material difference in people’s lives. This effort to connect with people’s material conditions has deep roots in socialist organizing. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, it was not uncommon for democratic socialist activists to join labor unions as a way to build stronger bonds with the working class. As a Jacobin article notes, these efforts echo today in institutions such as the union democracy group Teamsters for a Democratic Union and the publication Labor Notes . DSA similarly supports union organizing through its support for such institutions as the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee . Tenant organizing has now become an important vector of DSA activity alongside labor. There is a history here as well. As John Altas, one of Shelterforce ’s founders, explains , Shelterforce itself was founded in 1975 in an environment in which “the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee and the National Lawyers Guild [were] engaged in tenant organizing in several cities across the country.” Shanti Singh, a member of DSA San Francisco who has long worked for Tenants Together , a statewide tenant coalition in California, says the 2008 housing crisis drove a resurgence of both tenant unions and DSA. “Everyone needs housing. … It’s a very easy way to connect people’s everyday lives to larger economic systems,” says Nicole Zimmerman, a member of DSA’s Montgomery County branch in Maryland, adding that this makes it an obvious entry point for power building and political education. “When you’re talking to tenants or talking about landlords, there’s a very clear class divide there. … There’s power in numbers and [in] bringing people together to take on the landlords.” Singh makes a similar point. “Rent eats first, right?” Sebastian Fernandez Giraldo, a member of DSA’s North Carolina Triangle chapter, argues that tenant organizing is an easier way for DSA chapters to reach working people than labor organizing because it doesn’t require organizers to first get employed at the worksite to be organized. Tenant organizing is also powerful, Fernandez Giraldo adds, because it “creates the opportunity for people [who might] otherwise [not] be in touch with each other to talk about their issues and to see how they have a lot in common.” A National Commitment The convergence of DSA and tenant organizing dates to 2016, when some local DSA chapters— including Asheville, North Carolina; Flagstaff, Arizona; the San Francisco Bay Area; Chicago; Des Moines; and New York City—launched local tenant organizing efforts. Nationally, DSA established its Housing Justice Commission in 2019 . Allison Geroi, a member of DSA’s Metro DC chapter and an organizer with its tenant organizing affiliate Stomp Out Slumlords , wrote in a description of DSA’s 2019 convention that there was support for tenant organizing but also a concern that a national resolution might lead the national body to push a favored approach and discourage local experimentation. This concern was addressed by an agreement that the “national housing group would function primarily as a space to share resources and develop a strategy for national targets, rather than a campaign-in-a-box that would be exported to locals.” By the time this language was developed, support was strong, but other delays made it “clear that we would not reach the housing section of the agenda.” Supporters felt strongly enough that housing should be a DSA priority that they “actually ran up to the stage right as the convention was about to end and pushed that resolution through,” recalls Singh, who was among the delegates who did so. In 2021, buoyed by an uptick in tenant organizing across the country in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the national DSA passed a resolution that established “housing justice, with a focus on tenant organizing, as a national priority campaign”; dedicated the equivalent of one full-time position of national staff time to support local tenant organizing efforts; and “establish[ed] a permanent and ongoing train-the-trainers education curriculum and regular intake of new organizers seeking to establish or strengthen tenant organizing programs in their chapters.” In 2022, DSA implemented that resolution by launching a national tenant organizer training program, the Emergency Tenants Organizing Committee (ETOC), which “connected with over a dozen DSA chapters to share experiences and learn about their on-the-ground local organizing.” By 2023 , it had trained 18 DSA chapters and mentored 14 new local tenant unions “from as far west as Honolulu to as far east as East Tampa.” Between 2023 and 2025 , nearly 300 tenant organizers participated in ETOC trainings, and DSA members contributed to the formation of eight new tenant unions. DSA’s support of tenant organizing was reinforced in 2023 through additional training, funding, and a commitment to translating organizing materials (especially into Spanish). In 2025 , the national convention committed to undertaking a national mapping assessment of tenant organizing capacity and sought to link workplace and tenant struggles under a nationwide campaign with the theme of: “Organize your workplace, organize your building.” B uilding Power, Community by Community Although tenant organizing has become a high priority at the national level, DSA is a highly decentralized organization in which local chapters have considerable autonomy; not all of them have made tenant organizing a core part of their work. Those that have embraced tenant organizing have adopted varied approaches, depending on their local conditions. Mark Firla, who actively participated in DSA and tenant organizing in Connecticut between 2020 and 2023, relates that he and some of his fellow DSA members realized that there were unutilized state and local tenant protections on the books that they could use to generate interest among tenants and help them flex their political muscles. For example, a state statute allows the formation of local fair rent commissions to examine and eliminate excessive rental charges, and New Haven, where Firla lives, has had one since 1984. More than 70 percent of New Haven’s population are renters. This means the city has considerable, if latent, tenant political power. Firla says DSA worked to activate that power by “literally cold knocking doors and saying, ‘Hey, who’s your landlord? Do you have issues? Are they responsive?’” and then pushing the city to implement or enforce preexisting rules. This had concrete effects in terms of increasing local political power; it enabled the chapter to position itself to help lead a lobbying effort to pass a statewide right-to-counsel law in 2021. “One of the outcomes that the state has seen over the last three, four, five years is much more significant involvement [among] organized tenants,” says Firla, which, he adds, is likely why a lot more cities in the state now have fair rent commissions. But from a DSA perspective, Firla says, the power-building opportunity that tenant organizing provides has largely been squandered in the state. “If you’ve got a town of 20,000 people … and you have 200 organized community members or tenants, and those folks are willing to go work for a politician or work against a politician … they’re going to have a profoundly outsized impact,” he says. Instead, however, according to Firla, tenant organizers and DSA largely parted ways, and he argues that the state’s tenant organizing looks more like traditional lobbying. In Albany, New York, the relationship between DSA and the local tenant union has been much more symbiotic, according to Bebhinn Francis , who is both a Capital District DSA (CDDSA) member and lead tenant organizer at United Tenants of Albany (UTA). UTA, which was founded more than 50 years ago, is clearly independent of DSA. It receives its tenant union training from the Tenant Union Federation , not from DSA’s ETOC program, says Francis. But in terms of the actual work of forming and supporting tenant unions, UTA and CDDSA are highly integrated. Without DSA volunteers, UTA’s tenant union organizing program would effectively consist of only Francis. Francis goes so far as to say that without the work of CDDSA members, the local tenant movement “would not even exist.” With DSA volunteers, however, the situation is quite different. Working with CDDSA, Francis has helped lead eight large tenant union building campaigns, with the largest building housing 250 families. The people power from DSA greatly speeds operations: At one 150-unit building, Francis says, the team of door knockers from the CDDSA housing committee enabled organizers to amass 62 percent support for a tenant union in just three days. “CDDSA and I work hands-on throughout this process,” says Francis. “CDDSA helps with the outreach, the sign-ins. … When a tenant is afraid to give testimony for whatever reason … it’s a Capital District DSA member who reads that testimony on behalf of the tenant.” In North Carolina, the level of integration between DSA and tenant organizers is less pronounced than in Albany but more pronounced than in Connecticut. Another difference from Connecticut is that North Carolina lacked tenant-friendly policies or political environments at the state or local level. Therefore, the approach of making existing policies work for tenants was not available. Tenant and housing organizing in North Carolina, in short, often had to start from the ground up. Fernandez Giraldo joined the Raleigh branch of DSA’s North Carolina Triangle chapter in 2018 and became very active in Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign. After that campaign fell short, he saw the 2020 eviction moratorium as an extraordinary opportunity to reach people where they were and engage them politically. Fernandez Giraldo and a friend looked up addresses where evictions had been filed. “We figured out which ones were apartments,” he says, “and we would knock on every door in the apartment complex, and be like, ‘Hey, you’ve got these rights. There [are] also these resources that you can access.’” Slowly, he says, others within the DSA chapter joined in, eventually connecting with people in Chapel Hill and Durham to create the Triangle Tenant Union . The union includes DSA members, but it is institutionally autonomous. Fernandez Giraldo notes that the Raleigh City Council is “very right-wing, very controlled by real estate.” Other DSA chapters in North Carolina faced similar situations with their city councils, so they independently decided to focus on building tenant-union infrastructure and later linking up to create a statewide network of city- or regional-level groups. In 2024, with support from the Cypress Fund , a local philanthropic group , these groups formed the North Carolina Tenants Union . As with the Triangle Tenant Union, the tenant groups intentionally remain politically autonomous, even though many of their organizers are also DSA members. Perhaps ironically, given that the initial focus on tenant unions stemmed in part from local policy not looking promising, the new statewide tenant infrastructure is beginning to enable tenant organizing groups to advance policy at the local level. A major breakthrough occurred last fall in Durham, where, after years of tenant advocacy being stymied, the city council passed a resolution strengthening habitability rules . Tenant organizers are already mobilizing at the building level to remedy unsafe conditions. In Washington, D.C., the pandemic fueled a DSA chapter’s tenant organizing. Metro DC DSA already had a directly affiliated tenant organizing project, Stomp Out Slumlords , but it grew sharply from 2020 to 2021 , increasing from 13 to more than 40 organizers and from 7 to 20 sites. In fall 2025, tenants organized by Stomp Out Slumlords won a $41 million judgment in a case brought by the tenant association and the District of Columbia against the former owners of Marbury Plaza apartments in Anacostia. In her order , Superior Court Judge Yvonne Williams noted that mold remediation had been “required in 645 of 672 individual units and all 98 common areas.” Zimmerman says Montgomery County, Maryland, has focused first on achieving policy wins, notably the passage of a rent stabilization ordinance in 2023 , while D.C. proper has focused more on building tenant unions to stand up to landlords directly. Zimmerman serves on a coordinating committee that seeks to bridge the two strategies by advising the D.C. group on policy issues and connecting folks in Montgomery County with DSA Stomp Out Slumlords tenant organizers in D.C. when Maryland tenants are seeking to organize a building. In California regions with preexisting tenant organizing, such as the Bay Area and Los Angeles, the DSA chapters can directly channel electoral energy into housing, through initiatives such as right to counsel and taxing vacant apartment units. DSA San Francisco has enough political energy around housing to maintain two working groups, one on tenant organizing and one on social housing, says Singh. In other, more traditionally conservative regions of the state, such as the Central Valley, Inland Empire, and Orange County, Singh says, tenant unions are a newer phenomenon, and DSA chapters are helping many of them get off the ground. “Our dream,” she says, “is that every city in California above 100,000 people should have a tenant union.” Negotiating Tensions Firla notes that DSA chapters getting into tenant organizing face the familiar tension between pursuing the kinds of wins achievable by professional tenant association staff and the leadership development at the heart of successful long-term organizing. While the D.C. tenant union is an official DSA affiliate, this is not the norm. Formally, as stated in DSA’s 2025 housing justice resolution , the organization’s goal is “to create and strengthen tenant unions led democratically by rank-and-file tenants and not NGOs.” But maintaining a “rank-and-file” orientation can be easier said than done when funding often depends on philanthropy, with rank-and-file dues collections often secondary. A 2023 report from Stomp Out Slumlords captures this tension: “Organizational institutionalization in the current context virtually requires becoming a grant-seeking nonprofit and all of the restrictions on political advocacy and militancy that entails. At the outer limit of our hopes in 2021 was a collective entity with a thousand dues-paying members, but even if that were achieved and dues were set at $100 a year (well beyond most tenants’ actual willingness to pay), this would only support a single staff member and no office space.” According to Firla, in Connecticut, a lack of political education weakens the power that could come from tenant organizing. It’s “a really exciting opportunity,” he says, “if you can get folks to understand that same set of facts and have a broader understanding of who … we are as a community, and how we can exercise power that, in many cases, working people don’t understand they have.” Francis also emphasizes the importance of political education in maintaining alignment between DSA volunteers and tenants in tenant union organizing. “We’re really, really clear in our political education when we’re communicating with our tenants about lines of division and what class is,” she says. “There’s basically the ruling class and the working class. And even though our paychecks might vary in what they look like … we are all closer to the homeless side of this equation than the big CEO who’s owning these buildings, sitting in their mansion … in New Jersey.” Tenant Power Drives Electoral Wins DSA’s electoral ambitions have benefited from its focus on tenant issues. This may be particularly evident in New York, where DSA members have secured high-ranking political positions and advanced housing policy. For instance, State Sen. Julia Salazar , the first New York DSA member elected to the New York State Senate (in 2018), has consistently run on housing issues. In April 2026, Salazar introduced the Tenant Power Act to create legal protections for tenant unions. In New York City, a call to freeze the rent for rent-stabilized apartments—realized in late June—helped propel Mamdani to victory. In Washington, D.C., Aparna Raj , a DSA-backed tenant organizer, won the Democratic Party primary for city council in Ward 1 , typically tantamount to winning the general election. Her campaign, notes The 51 st , centered on housing and “addressing the District’s affordability problem.” Janeese Lewis George, D.C.’s Democratic mayoral nominee (and hence the city’s presumptive next mayor), is also a democratic socialist and won with the endorsement and active support of Metro DC DSA. In San Francisco, Singh notes, tenant and electoral organizing are often intertwined. “A lot of our electoral stuff has to do with housing,” she notes, including a ballot measure in 2026 that would raise $100 million for affordable housing in the city. As Singh says, “You can’t have economic [justice] and leave real estate capital untouched.” Steve Dubb is strategic initiatives editor at Shelterforce. Prior to Shelterforce, Steve worked as senior editor of economic justice at Nonprofit Quarterly. Before that, he worked at The Democracy Collaborative … and was also previously the executive director of NASCO (North American Students of Cooperation), a U.S. and Canadian association of housing cooperatives, focused on campus communities. Steve has authored and edited multiple books. Most recently, he co-edited (with Raymond Foxworth) Invisible No More: Voices from Native America (Island Press, 2023). Steve is based in Boston, Massachusetts, and actively volunteers in the area with multiple groups on economic justice work. The post Can Tenant Organizing Build Political Power? The DSA Experience appeared first on Working Mass . “}]]

articles.title: Organizing as Ancestral Practice: Building Infrastructure for the Next Era of Movements - The Forge
articles.content: As Judith LeBlanc, Executive Director of Native Organizers Alliance, and community organizer Jawanza Williams reflect to Guest Editor Kailea Loften, continuing to recognize that our power exists in the collective is the starting point. Building trust and meeting people must remain central to organizing best practices. As Judith shares, “organizing is about dealing with people who you don’t like, who’re not your bestie. It requires love, discipline, and a strategy to carry out. Discipline and love. People talk about love all the time, and I love love. But love is about discipline.” Kailea : What is organizing, and why do we organize? Judith: We’ve been organizing since the creator brought us into being. Our origin stories show that we’ve been organizing ourselves since dirt, since the beginning of time, because it is the only way to create community care and protection. It’s the only way that we can think about the future and the past, and move together in the present. Organizing is not a choice. I often think about our ancestral responsibilities to organize ourselves. I’m talking about all of our ancestors. Nelson Mandela, Mother Jones from the labor movement, Sitting Bull. You can name any place in the world, and there have always been people who have accepted our ancestral responsibilities to organize. Some people say — and I know it’s part of the ethos of the mainstream organizing movement, the Saul Alinsky kind of drive — that you organize to meet people’s needs no matter what it takes. I don’t believe that’s true. I think we do organize to meet people’s needs, but how we move defines why we move together. And the how has to be centered in the synergy between the heart and the mind. The soul and the physical needs. We need culture in how we do this work. That’s why we move together: alone, we cannot achieve very much. And capitalism as a system promotes the idea that there’s always one individual with a really bright idea, you know, like Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves. Sorry, not true. It was generations of people who organized. That means 40, 60, 80, 100 years of organizing. Jawanza: Organizing, to me, is a multidimensional practice of orienting oneself and recognizing and deepening value in other people. I came to organizing through my own direct needs as a young person living with HIV. I was experiencing homelessness. I needed access to health care and stable and secure housing. I happened to meet VOCAL New York at the particular time I was going through this experience. I became an organizer after being organized to save my life and others’ lives, and to improve the quality of our lives. But I quickly realized that organizing was about distilling the amorphous, wide-ranging principles of love, care, compassion, respect, and the honor of human beings into tangible parts that made sense. We can grapple with that and use it. That means having conversations, building relationships. It means producing culture. All the things that bring us back to center, that help us tap into what makes us truly human. I learned organizing through the Alinsky framing, but for me it’s truly about helping, not controlling or directing: helping to inform the force that we define right now as a social movement. This force of truth, this force that has been here since before 250 years ago, that has always been blasting us forward towards our collective destination and state of being. Those of us who decide to become organizers are helping to inform that force. Judith : You touched on something that I often return to when considering what supports our keeping on in the face of such tremendous obstacles and danger as there are now, which is love and care, respect and discipline. Organizing makes us more accountable to others. Movements are not controlled by any one person or group. And we’re in a period, almost a generation really, since the Iraq War, where you can see the growing acceptance that if something goes wrong in your community or in the world, you know you have the responsibility to get out on the street corners. During the Iraq War, there were thousands of little towns and big cities all across the U.S. and the world where people, on a weekly basis for years, would go out on the street corner to proclaim their opposition to a war based on lies and oil. Now it’s the No Kings movement. It’s not easy nor safe for many people, but they have chosen to be part of this big movement to say no to the Trump administration’s policies and to get out and make their own sites on the streets. How beautiful is that? So organizing is done by organizations that commit to it, but there’s a lot of self-organizing. Take a look at Minneapolis in response to the ICE surge. It proves that our traditional practices since the beginning of time have always been about organizing for community care and protection. You can’t have one without the other. If you’re going to have a sense of well-being, you also have to feel safe. It’s neighborhood kinship. Many people didn’t know one another, but they were ready to face incredible dangers to protect children from when they got off their school buses, to provide food, to patrol the streets. That proves that self-organizing and the fact that people understand movement, that they understand enough to create their own Signal channel, to be on alert, to be called into action at a moment’s notice. It’s all a testament to the fact that organizing was not discovered, like Plymouth Rock was, according to some. The rock was not the discovery of America. We’re in an era where organizations have to understand that this moment of people self-organizing is an amazing opportunity to do mass popular public education about the systemic roots of the crisis, because the problem is not Trump. The problem is the system and the very few who would use it to continue to profit and push the burden onto the majority, onto our backs, and onto our land. Kailea: I’m appreciating the framing of organizing as a traditional practice and how it helps us understand that this is nothing new. Being an active community member has always been about practicing agency and accountability to the collective. You have both worked for organizations focused on movement infrastructure over the years. Could you each explain why social movements need scaffolding? What conditions set us up to fall short, and what conditions create durability for our movements? Jawanza: Whenever I was a person being organized by organizers, I responded to a genuine practice of checking in, a genuine practice of creating community. When I first joined VOCAL- NY, we would have a general membership meeting every month at the same time, at the same place. There was a lot of organizing talk, a lot of campaign talk, a lot of talk about how are we going to get this bill passed, how are we going to get this politician to move this way or that. But the reason people return, and this is what became the focus for me as an organizer, is because it was a space where people wanted to be present. Where people wanted to come to be with other people. For thousands of years, we have gathered with our people. In the organizing context, we can expand who is considered our people and who is included in our people. We need to build a community practice of this, where we’re gathering not because you’re supposed to but because, when you come here, you are among family and friends. It’s a good feeling, and you don’t want to miss out. So how do you make that part of your regular organizing practice as a structural piece of how we do our work? There has to be space and time for breaking bread so that people can communicate and just be together. Our organizing scaffolding should be malleable, like bamboo. Bamboo is strong and durable, but it can bend, and organizing can bend based on the people who are a part of it. People do move on — sometimes they simply go to a new state and get a new job — so we need practices, stories, and ways of generating our work and ideas that outlive individuals and are permeable enough for new people to use and make their own. It’s important that people entering social movements or organizations do not have to reinvent the wheel. We should not assume that just because people have joined in, they know what they are doing. I was college-educated when I joined VOCAL, and I didn’t even know about organizing. So we need scaffolding to meet people as they come in. Judith : As the Lakota, Dakota people always say, you have to know where you come from to know where you are going. And I would add, therefore, know what to do in the present. At this time, at the 250th anniversary of the idea of America, it’s not the same as in past periods of history. Every period of history is unique. We have a situation where 70% of the people in this world live under the rule of totalitarianism. We are in the 30% who are fighting the consolidation of totalitarianism. There is a global context in the struggle that we are in now for human rights, to protect Mother Earth, to end the threat of war and destruction, to ensure people are not hungry. This is a global context. I think it’s decisive in a lot of ways. Social movements have a natural rhythm. When you look through history, there are times of great upsurge when the people go into the streets, take the power and win significant structural changes, or at least blunt the force of repression. But you can’t sustain being in the streets 24/7. Of course, there are examples of long-term struggles that ended with significant impact. For instance, during the Montgomery bus boycott, people walked and self-organized rides to work for over a year. In social movements, there are cycles of peaks and then periods when they slow down. In between those big peaks, organizations have the responsibility to consider how to help people sustain their awareness of what they’ve achieved and what the next steps are. Right now, we’re talking about a push for power that is called totalitarianism, and that is using any means necessary. We have never been this close to that kind of rule. The closest call was probably in the 50s when they were putting socialists and communists in jail for their beliefs. But even then, the people were able to push that back and to emerge into big movements in the 60s and the 70s. These peaks we’re in right now give us an opportunity to help people understand what is happening. We have to narrate — not tell them — narrate what we have done and how we can stay strong and continue forward. This happens through popular political education. And for many, election cycles are part of that educational process when you’re fighting totalitarianism. From my vantage point, elections don’t solve problems. They create different conditions under which we will solve the problems. In which we will organize. In which movements will grow. In 2020, we saw historic voter turnout across every community. It was the first time that Indigenous power was recognized by the political parties. We are a decisive electorate, but we were never considered that. But we flipped Arizona. And there are seven states where the native vote is a decisive swing vote. North Carolina has 330,000 natives. Nobody knows. Nobody talks about that. It is a decisive vote in Wisconsin, in Michigan, in Nevada; there are states that are considered by the political parties as swing states where a native vote is substantial and can make the difference. In 2020, we proved that through our actions and organizing in the wake of Standing Rock. In the wake of the 2018 election, the first two Indian women were elected to Congress. We never had our Barbara Lee or Maxine Waters. We never had that for our children. And so when we went into 2020, we were able to mobilize at the grassroots because representation matters. Representation isn’t a destination, but it matters. So when that election happened, it changed the conditions we were organizing within. We mobilized immediately after the election to put pressure on the transition team to nominate the first Indian woman to head the Department of the Interior. We knew that having an Indian woman in that position would lay the basis for us to organize for structural changes. So we got over 200 tribes and 19,000 people to immediately put the pressure on the transition team. They didn’t want her. They wanted an old white guy, but they were finally pressured to nominate her. It changed the conditions at the time. But the truth is, right now, the right wing has gained momentum, and their structural organizing has been going on for much longer than ours. I point to 2018 and 2020; that’s nothing. They’ve been organizing since the Goldwater campaign, when they began investing substantial resources in think tanks like the Cato Institute, running local elections, and creating their boilerplate for repressive legislation. Even if it wasn’t passed in the 60s, 70s, or 80s, or if it was and it was repealed, they have maintained a steady flow of resources. So why do we fall short? It’s not for lack of vision. It’s not for a lack of need or discipline. In my opinion, it’s a lack of understanding that there are no easy wins. Not everything can be solved in the short term. We need a long-term arc. But we don’t think that way. We’re always thinking about the next thing. And of course, we face the pressures of hunger and deprivation. We haven’t built, as Scott Nakagawa would say, a river of resistance. What we’ve done is stay in our streams, doing what we need in silos. The second thing I think causes us to fall short of resources is money. In Indian country, we get less than 1% of all philanthropic giving . The Black community, less than 5%. So resources, yes, to build programming, but more so for the human resources. We don’t put enough emphasis on the grassroots people. That’s what we’ve got to learn from L.A., Chicago, DC, and Minneapolis. People are the power. And so building relationships at the community level, where you grow that circle of trust, is what enables really militant, disciplined action to change policies. Which leads me to the last point. People have talked for many years, many decades, about base building. What does that really mean? It means that you are actually in relationships with people that you might not like, relationships with people that you might not agree with. But you are in relationships with people because you understand where power is. And that power cannot be exercised across differences unless you build trust and a shared understanding that together we’re stronger. That’s base building. It’s not mobilization; it’s organizing a base. And that organizing is about dealing with people who you don’t like, who’re not your bestie. It requires love, discipline, and a strategy to carry out. Discipline and love. People talk about love all the time, and I love love. But love is about discipline. King said it himself: power without love is abusive. I’m not discovering Plymouth Rock here. This is the truth. A recent example is the ten-year struggle to stop the Keystone XL pipeline. We were involved on the ground in Seattle in the last five years, and what was the key? It was grassroots, tribal, and the alliances with white ranchers and farmers. And the only basis for that alliance was their understanding of the natural world. They felt about the river the same way that we do. Maybe not for the same reasons, but they felt that the river was a living thing that needed our protection and that we could only protect it together. That’s what enabled us to win after 10 years. The stopping of that pipeline. So the base building there was among people we didn’t think we had a common cause with, among people that we didn’t think felt the same way we did about the natural world. We had to make alliances and make kinship with people who had, in the initial analysis, stolen our land three or four generations ago. And on the other side of the table, we have to say that’s the past. Right now, this is what we can do together to protect what is critical. The river. Jawanza : Judith, while you were talking about base building and about recognizing that people may value the same thing for different reasons, I reflected that when I’m organizing I have to be able to discuss issues across different contexts. I have to meet people where they are. Part of this is also helping people develop new ways of seeing the world. Helping people see their own identity, their own experiences. I’m also always looking to see who’s missing in the conversation. And I work to go find them to bring them in. That’s discipline. It’s hard. It slows things down. But it should be a fundamental goal of any structure you’re building for your organizing project. Kailea: I’m appreciating how both of you get to the heart of the ideas and the frameworks that can feel big and challenging to approach. I’m hearing that, at the core, it’s about taking the time to understand what people value, which means we have to meet people with real curiosity and a level of earnestness. It’s clear that we do need to lower the cost of onboarding and collaboration when inviting and bringing people into our movements. How do we do this? Jawanza: The entry threshold needs to be as low as possible. Base-building projects need to be about identifying potential leaders, identifying issues impacting communities, and offering a worldview, rather than telling people what to think. People who are in crisis should be able to participate. When I was experiencing homelessness, I had also just recently been diagnosed HIV positive, and I was in New York, which was a new city, by myself. I’d never been to a big city before. It was crazy. If it had been difficult for me to join, for instance, if I had had to prove myself, I would have felt excluded. And we’re supposed to be the people coming together to fight exclusion. We also need a low barrier to re -engagement if people fall off the project. One thing I really appreciate about organizing with VOCAL New York is that there are two tiers of membership. There are the general members, which include everyone who is impacted by the issues. General members inform us about what’s going on. They help us understand what communities are experiencing firsthand. The second tier is also made up of people from the general membership, but they have committed to advancing this work and to bringing new people in. These positions are non-staff positions at this organization. You’re a person, just like me, who’s experiencing different things, and you’ve decided to be transformed by this work. As a last point, when I’m bringing new people in, I diversify how people consume information. I screen videos before the meetings even start, of people, for instance, in an action, so you can see what’s going on. I’ll have music playing, but I’m always intentional about the music and lyrics. I’m considering all of this as part of how I build an inclusive room for everyone we are trying to get in there. This even ties into public transportation infrastructure, because how people will get to the meeting is important to consider. Judith : I would love to spend some time interrogating the idea of movement spaces. I think it has always struck me as exclusive, whereas movements are so broadly inclusive that people, you know, who never did anything before suddenly make a sign. That’s a movement. And I was thinking: If we were to interrogate and define what movement spaces are, then maybe we would have a different approach to the structure of organizations and to our relationships with the communities in which we serve, because organizations inherently are not movement spaces. That’s what the Native Organizers Alliance does: we support the leaders, the organizations, and the movements. The Keystone XL movement, the Standing Rock movement, the movement for representation in government. I just came from Minneapolis. I’ve been there a few times during the surge. I have family there. My sister-in-law teaches in the neighborhood where the surge was happening in the Indian community. And we have had partnerships with one particular organization for nearly a decade. I also used to live there in the 70s during Wounded Knee. So I have a lot of ties. I know the history and the grandchildren of people. So if you’re sitting in Minneapolis, and you’re in an organization that supported the movement because there wasn’t one organization that set up these Signal channels, or the food distributions, or the rides for students, or the patrolling. It emerged citywide and in Saint Paul. Some organizations became hubs where people could come, rest, and figure out what’s going on. There were hubs where people could pick up food. There’s still ICE there; they’re not totally gone. But the people’s power forced a change in tactics and compelled the government to remove those who were there representing the federal government, and ultimately, you know, got rid of Secretary Noem, the former governor of South Dakota. So what do we do now? We had a day-long discussion with the organization we partnered with about how to encourage and engage people from the movement. What is it that we initiate that can continue to build a connected relationship? What is it that can be done culturally, politically, and spiritually? What are the elements? And then how do we give them opportunities to connect with the movement? Because these people took action and became even more prepared for the next time. This is not a one-off. If you’re thinking about a 20- to 40-year struggle to stop totalitarian and totalitarianist governance, then you’ve got to be thinking about how to build trust. You can’t be event-driven now. You’ve got to be purpose-driven now to consolidate the relationships between people who moved by their hearts and took incredible action under duress. How do you keep them in a relationship around your organization? Because that’s the only power you have. You can’t create a movement space. The space you have is the role you played in the community and the accountability you’ve had to the community. The group we have partnered with for 10 years has a 35-year history in the native community and is known and trusted. So how do you use that position and accountability in the community to create these broader circles around you who will be prepared to take urgent action the next time? Kailea: There is so much to glean here. Before we close, any last thoughts? Jawanza: Trust that if you help develop the people, the movements will manifest. We do this by identifying the values we want to uphold in our hearts and minds for how we work. And remember, that it’s not just about your organization. Judith: This time, it’s not like the past. This is a time when we must think about the next 20 to 40 years as it relates to our everyday practical work as organizations. It’s going to be hard for some to lead with both our hearts and ideology, our souls and worldview, because you can’t separate one from the other. But we must if we are to have the discipline and courage to confront rising totalitarianism. And third, movements make change. That’s a proven social fact. And they must change organizations and how we organize. We must learn the lessons that movements teach us. When masses of people take action, we have to study it. We have to analyze what it means for how we do our work going forward as organizers and organizations. Because in the final analysis, people have the power, and when they’re in motion, we can learn some valuable lessons about when, why, and how we organize.

articles.title: Class Traitors Are Welcome in the Socialist Movement
articles.author: Noah Suárez-Sikes
articles.content: We are in a moment of particular fascination with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) across the nation. With the victory of congressional candidates like Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Chris Rabb, and Melat Kiros, DSA has arrived on the political stage, proving that the election of Zohran Mamdani was not a fluke but a harbinger of a growing movement. Outlets like Fox News have seized on all sorts of DSA content, from interviewing cochairs and National Political Committee members to, for some reason, breathlessly reporting on a Y2K-themed prom fundraiser thrown in Los Angeles.That coverage took a turn last week, with the press and pundits obsessing over Gustavo Gordillo, the democratically elected cochair of the New York City chapter of DSA, a thirty-eight-year-old former union electrician who has had his personal life suddenly put under a microscope as if he were Princess Diana. He’s not the first; it’s happened to other DSA leaders before him, such as Cea Weaver.Over the past week, local and national media have desperately tried to get readers and viewers to care that Gordillo lives in a house purchased by his father. A New York Times profile quickly turned into a long investigative saga by multiple outlets; for some reason, the local public radio station’s outlet Gothamist trekked to an anarchist bookstore to ask patrons about the story. (Spoiler: turns out nobody there really cared.) Numerous column inches have been dedicated to this story; city council members have weighed in; journalists now are camping outside the Brooklyn row house. Maybe the paparazzi will be outside the next chapter meeting.The intent here is to delegitimize DSA by “exposing” the “hypocrisy” of its leaders. But it’s not quite clear what the “gotcha” is supposed to be. The underlying message seems to be that Gordillo shouldn’t believe in and be organizing for a better, more equitable world because his father, like most parents who have worked hard throughout their lives, wanted to leave his children (Gordillo and his brother) with the economic stability that a house provides.The home was, according to the Times’ reporting, purchased in 2019 at barely above the median home price in Brooklyn at the time — hardly the stuff of the ultrawealthy. Even with its appreciation since then, the house is less than a third of the threshold of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s new pied-à-terre tax, on second homes worth over $5 million. (And, of course, the house is not a second home.) This is, unfortunately, just what homes tend to cost these days, which one would think the Times would know.But even if we were talking about a 1 percenter here, what’s the upshot? That someone who is leading a relatively comfortable life has chosen not to zealously defend that wealth and selfishly bask in its splendor but rather to fight for a world where everyone is able to have their needs met? Sounds like a good thing to me.Of course, from the New York Times to Rupert Murdoch’s press, these are institutions that largely express elite concerns, and elites are not happy about the rise of socialist politics in this country. They dress up these attacks in the language of “hypocrisy,” with the implication that because we are a socialist organization, we want to hunt down every moderately comfortable person with torches and pitchforks. Obviously that’s not true, and they know it; even the most ambitious DSA program advocates a world with an equitable, democratic economy. We advocate that those with means contribute more, and we’re happy to have anyone who believes in that goal of a better world participate in our project — even someone who, God forbid, owns a home.If you asked me to psychoanalyze the reactionary commentariat, I’d say their guilty conscience is resurfacing as they’re forced to consider why someone who isn’t struggling themselves would have the audacity to want to help others. These people, many of whom are from far more privileged backgrounds, feel ashamed to think that they could be doing more with their class position — that they in fact owe it to others to do more. In response to such anxieties, they turn to retribution. Maybe an enterprising journalist should take up such questions with the authors of these pieces on Gordillo.The Murdoch press love to facilitate this kind of pile-on. They have a particular obsession with whipping up a hate frenzy against particular DSA members to make examples of people fighting capital. For example, the New York Post recently attacked Grace Ryan, who has supported progressive New York congressional candidate Brad Lander and volunteered as a DSA organizer, for her father’s background as the owner of a chocolate company.Socialists shouldn’t be fazed by these attacks. Many leaders on the broad left, from Marxists to liberals, emerged from a downwardly mobile professional class — some frustrated with a fragile class position, others perfectly comfortable in their wealth.Vladimir Lenin, Maximilien Robespierre, Mahatma Gandhi, and Fidel Castro all studied law. Leon Trotsky was originally a mathematician and mechanical engineer. Simón Bolívar came from one of the wealthiest families in the Americas; Rosa Luxemburg came from a well-off family in Russian-occupied Poland. Che Guevara was a doctor. Giuseppi Garibaldi was a teacher; Giuseppe Mazzini was, you guessed it, a lawyer.Even the earliest socialists were class traitors: Friedrich Engels came from a wealthy business family and used that wealth to support Karl Marx. And Marx’s father? Another lawyer.We could go on and on. Franklin Delano Roosevelt came from a famously patrician family yet oversaw the greatest expansion of social welfare and other pro-worker policies in American history.These figures took up progressive politics and organizing because they saw social injustices they wished to correct. Looking behind the curtain of their deeply unequal societies revealed to them the exploitative and brutal nature of the system, even if they were benefiting from it. Confronted by the failure of the institutions that once supported their class, they made a choice — a choice to fight on behalf of others.These figures subsequently became part of mass movements composed of all class backgrounds, and that is what DSA represents today. Obviously Gordillo is not Simón Bolívar. (At least not yet — there’s always time!) But he is a representative of a fast-growing, mass movement, one of many leaders from various class backgrounds who form a bloc of diverse organizers.I live in Los Angeles and organize with the DSA chapter here. I attended what may generously be called an “elite institution,” the University of Southern California, on scholarship. But I have comrades within the organization who have been undocumented or homeless. DSA’s elected officials come from all walks of life: our slate of DSA-LA electeds includes Hugo Soto-Martinez, a champion for workers and tenants who is the son of street vendors, a former union organizer, and the sole renter on city council.It’s been a very long time since the United States saw a socialist movement of this size, and DSA is in its relative infancy. That this movement includes people of all stripes shows the breadth of the demand for societal change. The obsession with the class position of a few members pretends that the fight for socialism is simply an elite concern that ordinary people do not understand. Not only is this not true, it is backward: socialism is a concern for the shared humanity of everyone, a concern that those from “comfortable” walks of life can also come to grasp.These ideas are increasingly understood by people of all walks of life. We know 58 percent of Democrats have a positive view of democratic socialism, and 46 percent of all Americans ages eighteen to thirty-four view democratic socialism positively. And democratic socialists are winning over voters of color: Claire Valdez won every age bracket and racial group in her district, Darializa Avila Chevalier decisively won black voters in her district, and incumbent democratic socialists like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib have long represented majority-minority districts.It is because of our growing power that the establishment is trying so hard to discredit this movement. From Los Angeles to New York, the same attacks are being recycled against the Left by a rotating group of talking heads. But socialism is growing because it’s rooted in the real, material struggles of peoples’ lives.That movement has to have workers at its core. I also hope it includes socialist chocolate heiresses who want to knock doors and former sculpture Master of Fine Arts students. It’s a testament to the strength and appeal of the organization that we take all sorts, and it’s a testament to how out of touch the establishment is that these are the attacks they’re forced to trot out.Gordillo may be living in a house his father bought him. But it’s DSA that’s living rent-free in our critics’ heads.

articles.title: Farm Labor in NY – Immigration Raids and Unionizing
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: By Elizabeth Henderson As farms in NY come under increasing economic pressure with rising costs, stagnant or shrinking revenues, and ICE raids and deportations, the farm labor dilemma – who is going to do the work and under what conditions – gains greater urgency. Some farms have turned to H2A, bringing in guest workers from Jamaica, Mexico, and even Egypt. Since H2A is restricted to seasonal jobs, dairy farms cannot use it, and as a result, many rely on undocumented workers. Knowingly hiring an undocumented worker is a felony; farmers use various strategies to not “know,” even as everyone in a small town is aware of which farms have undocumented workers. Mainstream agricultural organizations are focusing on expanding the H2A program, lowering the pay rate and legal protections. Farmworkers are turning to unions. NY is one of only 5 states where farmworkers are legally allowed to unionize. The federal law, the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, that allows workers to bargain collectively excludes domestic workers and farmworkers, most of whom were African-American at the time of passage, and the law has not been amended since. The 2019 NYS Farmworkers Fair Labor Practices Act (FFLPA) established: collective bargaining rights for farmworkers, including H2A workers (approximately 12,000 of the 82,000 NY farmworkers); a weekly day of rest; unemployment insurance, disability benefits, and worker’s compensation; housing inspections applied to all employer-provided housing; and overtime wages of time-and-a-half for any work performed over 60 hours a week that ratchets down over ten years to 40 hours a week to match jobs in other sectors. The unionizing process is overseen in NYS by the Public Employees Relations Board (PERB) that mainly oversees public service workers’ unions, (teachers, police, firemen). There was so much uproar and effective organizing from NYS farmers that the state implemented a tax benefit for farmers that covers the overtime. Farmers have to apply to get this tax break that pays for the added expense of overtime. At least 3 unions have been organizing on farms (the United Farm Workers (UFW), the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), and the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union (RWDSU), focusing on larger fruit and vegetable farms that tend to have more workers. UFW has received certification and signed contracts with Cahoon Farms and A&J Kirby Farms. Negotiations are stalled between UFW and the Brooklyn Grange , an organization with rooftop farms in Brooklyn (135,000 square feet under cultivation) and other parts of the city that also designs and maintains gardens and claims to use exclusively organic practices. The workers, who only work 6 months a year, are asking for $26 an hour. The MIT living wage calculator puts the Brooklyn wage at $29.25 an hour, but that’s for year-round work for a single individual. The NY Vegetable Growers Association challenged the law in court and lost. The challenge aimed at the inclusion of H2A workers in the unions. The Vegetable Growers are appealing this judgment. Waffler Farms in Wayne County refused to negotiate, took the UFW to court for not allowing the farmer to present his opposition to the union to the workers, and lost, so has had to accept a contract. This video of Waffler yelling at his workers went viral and may shed some light on why they chose to unionize: bit.ly/waff-vid . Under the FFLPA, workers can sign cards authorizing a union to represent them and agreeing to pay union dues. If over 50% of the workers sign cards, the FFLPA does not require that there also be an election. Whether a card check or an election is more democratic is hotly contested with unions and worker advocates saying that the card check gives workers a better chance to express what they want free of employer pressure, and employers claiming that without the election, workers do not get to choose freely since union organizers may be pressuring workers to sign cards or even misleading them about what signing means. Historically, it is during the run-up to union elections that employers use all their powers to dissuade workers from voting for the union, including special meetings with workers, intimidation, and threats of firing or deporting workers who vote union or closing the business rather than accept a contract. Under state and federal regulations, these are unfair labor practices; however, when workers file official complaints, investigations take years. For farmworkers there is a long history of employer abuse, wage theft, and even human trafficking as well as the inherent imbalance of power between workers and employers that At-Will law entails. (NY and 48 other states have At-Will law that allows an employer to fire an employee without cause, though there are limits such as illness or discrimination by age or ethnicity.) The federal Department of Labor has Wage Division inspectors who investigate cases of wage theft if there is a complaint, but the number of inspectors is at an all-time low. Employers stand less than a 1% chance of undergoing an investigation. Many workers believe that a union contract is a more certain way to ensure that the employer will pay them full wages and benefits. The FFLPA allows workers to authorize a union via the card check process. If the employer challenges the card check, then an election takes place as occurred March 27, 2025 on Merrell Dairy Farm in Wayne County. The union, UFCW Local 1, lost 44 to 2. Collective bargaining through a union means that all the workers in the bargaining unit receive whatever benefits the contract with the employer includes. While individual workers might sometimes be able to negotiate better deals for themselves because of outstanding talent, hard work, or good relations with the employer, many workers believe that there is safety and greater strength in numbers. Is card check less democratic than an NLRB-officiated election? Card check , also called majority sign-up , is a method for employees to organize into a labor union in which a majority of employees in a bargaining unit sign authorization forms, or “cards”, stating they wish to be represented by the union. Since the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) became law in 1935, card check has been an alternative to the National Labor Relations Board ‘s (NLRB) election process. Card check and election are both overseen by the National Labor Relations Board or in NYS by the PERB. The difference is that with card sign-up, employees sign authorization cards stating they want a union, the cards are submitted to the NLRB and if more than 50% of the employees submit cards, the NLRB requires the employer to recognize the union and proceed to negotiate a contract. The employer may not know that employees are signing cards until the announcement that 50% has been surpassed. The NLRA election process is an additional step with the NLRB or the PERB conducting a secret ballot election after authorization cards are submitted. In both cases the employer never sees the authorization cards or any information that would disclose how individual employees voted. An employer can agree to leave the decision about joining a union entirely to the employees by accepting a neutrality agreement . The employer agrees to remain neutral during the union organizing campaign. This typically means they will not actively campaign against the union, express opinions about union representation, or interfere with employees’ decisions about unionization. Which workers are in a bargaining unit? Another hotly contested issue is the definition of the bargaining unit: which workers should be included in the union? Should year-round workers and temporary workers be in the same unit? Managers are not included in bargaining units with the workers they manage. Who classifies as a manager? Usually, employers and unions negotiate on this question. This was one of the issues at the Lynn-Ette and Sons Farm in Carlton, NY, where ICE arrested 14 farmworkers right off the bus that was taking them to work at the farm in May, 2025. What are union dues? Union dues are the monthly fees that members of a union pay to support the work of the union negotiating contracts, representing workers as individuals or in groups in cases of grievances of violations to the contract, accompanying workers in evaluation meetings with management if the worker so chooses, and reporting unfair labor practices to the NLRB or the PERB. Dues are the main source of union funding. Typically, unions do not have grants or federal funding. When a worker signs a card check, they agree to pay dues, but dues are not collected until the union negotiates and signs a contract with the employer . Dues for UFW membership are 3% of a worker’s wages. This amount was set by a vote of worker delegates to the UFW national convention in 2018. Since all the workers in a bargaining unit enjoy the benefits provided by a contract (wages, paid holidays, sick leave, etc.), it is considered fair that they all pay union dues. This is the language of the FLFLP bill : AN ACT to amend the labor law, in relation to granting collective bargaining rights to farm laborers and allowing farm workers one day of rest each week and including farm laborers within the provisions pertaining to overtime compensation and unemployment insurance; to amend the public health law, in relation to the application of the sanitary code to all farm and food processing labor camps for migrant workers; to amend the workers’ compensation law, in relation to the eligibility of farm laborers for workers’ compensation benefits and the provision of claim forms to farm laborers injured in the course of employment and in relation to service as farm laborers; and to amend the labor law, in relation to labor on a farm and regulating the employment of certain employees whose earning capacity is affected or impaired by youth or age. H2A Expansion In 2024 growers recruited 384,000 H-2A workers (a sixth of the country’s farm labor workforce), mostly from Mexico, under temporary work contracts. These laborers can only work for the grower who recruits them, and can be fired and deported for protesting, organizing or because the manager thinks they are working too slowly. Towards the end of the Biden administration in April 24, Julie Su, Biden’s Secretary of Labor, and well-meaning staffers put forward the Farmworker Protection Rule, a revised Rule for the H2A program that attempted to redress some of the worst abuses that complaints or investigative reporting had revealed. The Rule allowed H2A workers to freely receive visitors in farm-provided housing, including union representatives, required seat belts in all vehicles transporting H2A workers, opened the possibility of unionization for H2A workers, and clarified requirements for the work orders that specify wages and work assignments. Biden’s DOL also implemented the Farm Labor Stabilization Act, $50 million in grants to farms to pay for improvements to housing and wage hikes if the farms hired H2A workers from Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador. Paused along with many other agricultural program funding in early 2025, farms report receiving promised funds for this one. For over 20 years, the Farm Labor Organizing Committee (FLOC) has successfully organized H2A workers on over 600 farms in North Carolina, despite constant attacks from the Right to Work Foundation. FLOC conducted a successful campaign against Campbell Soup’s captive supply contracts with the farms that resulted in higher payments to the farms with guaranteed passthrough to FLOC’s farmworker members. At the end of June, 2025, DOL scrapped the Farmworker Protection Rule. With its elimination, growers are free to bar outsiders (community groups or unions) from labor camps, give workers contracts in languages they can’t read, retaliate against workers who complain of bad conditions, and even stop using seat belts in the vehicles transporting laborers to the fields. Greeted by overwhelming support from big ag, the current administration has promised to make H2A even more grower-friendly. The secretary of agriculture, Brooke Rollins, told Congress that she’d modernize the H-2A program “to do everything we can to make sure that none of these farms or dairy producers are put out of business [by immigration enforcement].” Effective October 2, 2025, DOL implemented a new rule that lowers H2A wages by changing the way the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (that is supposed to prevent H2A from undercutting domestic farmworker wages) is calculated. The result is a reduction in wages from $3 to $7 an hour depending on the state, and allows farmers to charge an “Adverse Compensation Adjustment,” code-speak for weekly payments for housing. The rule sets up two skill-based tiers for wages. If employers would have hired an untrained person for a job, they can pay the lower rate, even though the person they actually hire has years of experience. In November, 2025, the UFW Foundation and 18 individual farmworkers sued to stop the wage cuts. In May 2026, a federal district court denied their request for a preliminary injunction to stop the cuts, so they will continue while the case works its way through the courts. The suit argues that the wage cut rule violates the federal statute that requires that H2A not have an adverse effect on the jobs and wages of local workers. The UFW claims that the wage cut transfers over $4 billion dollars a year in wages from workers to employers. Keep in mind that over half the H2A visas are held, not by individual farmers, but by Farm Labor Contractors who have been found guilty of the worst abuses , including wage theft, miserable housing, and even human trafficking. DOL claimed that this new rule will save employers over $24 billion over the next decade, in effect confirming the UFW claim. Not surprisingly, farm employers and the Farm Bureau crowed with delight. Codifying the Wage Cuts into Law In June, 2026, G. T. Thompson, Republican chair of House Ag Committee submitted Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act (SAWA), claiming that this bill will correct the problems for agriculture that the current administration policies on immigration have caused. But the bill goes much farther by codifying in law the October 2025 DOL Rule that lowered the wages for H2A workers. SAWA keeps Sec. Rollins’ promise to expand H2A by including processing workers as well as farmworkers in the H2A category, expanding contracts from a maximum of 10 months to 3 years, allowing staggered entry of workers to fit a farmer’s schedule, permitting workers to shift from one certified farm or Farm Labor Contractor to another, and streamlining the whole application process that has taken up to 3 months involving contacts with five different government agencies into one on-line platform. To further consolidate and rationalize the system, SAWA charges the Secretary of Labor with creating an online registry of farm jobs and a database of all H2A jobs. While the UFW took part in negotiations that resulted in the Farm Workforce Modernization Act (FWMA), a previously proposed bill that did not pass, no farmworkers had any say in SAWA. It is an agribusiness bill carefully designed to cement the exploitative working conditions, low wages, and disempowerment of farmworkers that undermine the sustainability, not to mention the social justice, of agriculture in the US. Flawed though the proposed process was, FWMA provided a path to legal status for farmworkers and their families. SAWA does not throw farmworkers even these meager scraps. It does provide a way for farmworkers who have been working without full legal status to qualify as H2A workers without leaving the country, but to qualify for a waiver of deportation, current farmworkers not only have to document with the help of their employer that they worked 5.75 hours a day for 180 days over 2 years, they must also never have accessed any public benefits or have any record of other crimes besides working illegally. There is no mention of the fate of other members of farmworker families. Upon termination, H2A workers have 30 days to leave the country, reduced from the previous 60-day limit. The bill lets employers who previously employed undocumented workers off the hook for the felony charge this would currently entail. Responding to farmer complaints during the most recent government shutdown, processing of H2A applications will continue even if the government does not pay DOL bureaucrats! On wages, SAWA establishes two tiers – entry level with a lower base wage and specialized skills with a higher wage, but there is an additional nasty twist. If an employer would have hired an unskilled person for a job classified as entry level, but hires someone with years of experience, they can still pay the wage they would have paid to a totally inexperienced worker. (You have to stay up late at night to conjure up these miserly measures.) In Thompson’s introduction to the bill, he responds to farmer complaints of uncertainty about the required wage rate: “Wages for H-2A workers are calculated based on the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR), a minimum wage originally designed to ensure domestic workers were not undercut by foreign laborers. Dubious methodologies saw this rate skyrocket from 2010 – 2025 – in this time period, the increases to the AEWR outpaced inflation by 70%.” The historical record shows, however, that DOL under Biden was making an effort to raise farmworker wages from the federal minimum of $7.25 to something resembling a living wage. The loudest complaints came from farmers and especially Farm Labor Contractors who had been enjoying their freedom to outrageous exploitation. The bill also responds to complaints of uncertainty about the required wage rate by mandating that the wage rate cannot go more than 1.5% lower or 3.25% higher than the previous year. As under the current system, employers must provide housing, and the housing must be inspected by state entities using state standards for health and safety if they exist or, in the absence of state standards, the federal requirements. However, the employer is no longer required to provide the housing free of charge. The Secretary of Labor will set the maximum daily charge with a formula for calculating it (See text of bill p. 6: section E Provision Expense). Requiring that employers demonstrate some attempt to hire locals, SAWA continues the fiction that H2A workers are not taking jobs from US residents. And if a local pops up before the H2A workers start their journey, the farm must cancel the H2A visa. The huge growth in H2A visas to over 400,000 in 2025 suggests that no one is making a genuine effort to make farmwork a respected vocation that attracts citizens. Under SAWA, employer certification to hire H2A is renewable and may be filed by two or more employers in association or by cooperatives. If a group is the “permitted filer” and is barred from certification for abusing workers, the individual farms in the group can still continue in the program. Unlike the previous requirement that employers provide at least 75% of the hours listed in the contract, the bill does not require employers to provide a set number of hours of work. There is no weekly minimum or maximum beyond 1 hour during every 30-day period. So workers could be left with barely any earnings. Thompson responds to news of worker deaths from heat exposure by requiring that H-2A-certified farms have a heat plan. With unabashed cynicism, the bill calls for “prevention measures that are at least as protective as the applicable Federal and State requirements” and to post it where workers can see it. The authors are surely aware that neither the feds nor most states have heat protection legislation. No enforcement of the heat plan is required either. There is no question that Thompson’s bill responds to the urgent requests of mainstream agriculture. The American Farm and an assortment of 400 agriculture organizations endorse it. Like sugar, exploitation is addictive. Yet like too much sugar in your diet, stealing from the most marginalized makes US agriculture sick. How collaborative do you imagine relations will be on the farms that invite the H2A workers they have been depending on to return for a lower wage with fees for housing? Workers across the food chain and the many people who want healthy food must reject SAWA along with the Republican House and Senate draft Farm Bills. To solve the farm labor dilemma requires a major social movement that uplifts the voices of farmworkers, farmers on all scales, as well as workers across the food chain, labor organizations, and conscious eaters. We can envision an organic agriculture that is ethical, rigorous, and free of complicity in the neoliberal profit-driven economy. Another agriculture is possible.
